variants.stem: Which gland secretes thyroxine, a hormone that regulates the body's metabolic rate?
Which endocrine gland, located in the anterior neck, controls the rate of metabolism?
T₃ and T₄ are produced by which gland?
Which gland's hormones set the body's basal metabolic rate?
A shortage of iodine can cause an enlarged gland in the neck. Which gland is affected?
Which gland takes up iodine to make hormones that control cellular metabolism?
Which gland is stimulated by TSH from the pituitary and regulates metabolism?
Which butterfly-shaped gland wraps around the front of the trachea?

questions.why: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃), which regulate the body's metabolic rate.
questions.deep: The pituitary releases thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which tells the thyroid to release its hormones (a negative feedback loop). Iodine is needed to make thyroid hormones. The parathyroid glands, behind the thyroid, regulate calcium.

variants.stem: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the kidneys, producing more concentrated urine?
Released from the posterior pituitary, which hormone helps the body conserve water?
A person is dehydrated. Which hormone's release increases to reduce urine output?
Which hormone is also called vasopressin?
Which hormone makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water?
Which hormone decreases after a person drinks a large amount of water, resulting in dilute urine?
Which hormone regulates the body's water balance by acting on the kidneys?
Alcohol inhibits the release of which hormone, leading to increased urination?

questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released when the body needs to conserve water. It makes the kidney's collecting ducts more permeable to water so more is reabsorbed.
questions.deep: ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Higher ADH = less urine, more concentrated. Lower ADH = more urine, dilute. Memory aid: ADH = Anti-Diuretic Hormone (anti-peeing).

variants.stem: Which protein in red blood cells binds oxygen for transport?
The iron-containing protein that gives red blood cells their color is:
Oxygen is carried in the blood mainly by binding to which molecule?
Which molecule in erythrocytes carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues?
Anemia is often caused by too little of which oxygen-carrying protein in the blood?
Each red blood cell is packed with which iron-containing protein that picks up oxygen in the lungs?
Which protein is responsible for most of the oxygen transport in human blood?
Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds in place of oxygen to which protein?

questions.why: Hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein inside red blood cells, binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.
questions.deep: Each hemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) lack a nucleus, giving more room for hemoglobin. Albumin helps maintain blood osmotic pressure, and fibrinogen is involved in clotting.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which are functions of the skeletal system?
Select all that apply: The bones of the skeleton serve which purposes?
Select all that apply: Which of these does the skeletal system do?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are NOT functions of the skeletal system?
Select all that apply: Which functions does bone tissue perform?
Select all that apply: Which statements about the skeletal system are true?
opts: It protects the heart and lungs

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which tasks are carried out by bones?
Select all that apply: Which of the following does the skeleton provide?

questions.why: The skeletal system supports the body, protects organs, provides leverage for movement, stores minerals such as calcium and phosphorus, and houses red bone marrow, where blood cells are made.
questions.deep: Hematopoiesis (blood cell production) occurs in red bone marrow. Yellow bone marrow stores fat. The skeletal system does not digest food, exchange gases, filter blood, or make hormones such as insulin.

variants.stem: Where in the male reproductive system is sperm produced?
Spermatogenesis occurs within which structures of the testes?
Which coiled tubules inside the testes contain the cells that develop into sperm?
Sperm cells first form in which part of the testis?
Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis. Where are they initially produced?
Meiosis occurs in which male structures to form sperm?
Which structures make up most of the volume of the testes and produce sperm?
In which structures do spermatogonia divide and develop into sperm?

questions.why: Sperm are produced by meiosis in the seminiferous tubules, the coiled tubes inside the testes.
questions.deep: Sperm path: seminiferous tubules (made) → epididymis (matured and stored) → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra. The prostate gland and seminal vesicles add fluid to form semen. Testosterone is made by interstitial (Leydig) cells between the tubules.

variants.stem: Which structures filter lymph and contain lymphocytes that respond to pathogens?
Swollen glands in the neck during an infection are most likely enlarged:
Lymph passes through which small, bean-shaped structures before returning to the bloodstream?
Which lymphatic structures trap pathogens from lymph fluid?
Which structures are clustered in the armpits, neck, and groin and filter lymph?
Macrophages and lymphocytes inside which structures remove foreign particles from lymph?
Which part of the lymphatic system filters lymph, in contrast to the spleen, which filters blood?
Which small, bean-shaped organs are located along lymphatic vessels?

questions.why: Lymph nodes are bean-shaped structures along lymphatic vessels that filter lymph, trapping pathogens so macrophages and lymphocytes can destroy them.
questions.deep: Lymph nodes cluster in the neck, armpits, and groin and swell during infection as immune cells multiply. The spleen filters blood and removes old red blood cells. The thymus is where T cells mature.

variants.stem: Which of the following is NOT a macromolecule?
Which of the following is a monomer rather than a macromolecule?
All of the following are macromolecules EXCEPT:
Which is the building block (monomer) that links together to form large carbohydrates?
Which of these is a simple sugar and not a polymer?
Which of the following is NOT a large molecule built from many smaller repeating units?
Starch, glycogen, and cellulose are macromolecules made of repeating units of which smaller molecule?
Which one is NOT considered a macromolecule?

questions.why: Glucose is a single simple sugar (a monomer). Macromolecules are large polymers built from many monomers: starch and glycogen from glucose, proteins from amino acids, and DNA and RNA from nucleotides.
questions.deep: Four macromolecule types: carbohydrates (monomer: monosaccharide), lipids (fatty acids and glycerol; not true polymers), proteins (amino acids), and nucleic acids (nucleotides). Starch, glycogen, and cellulose are all long chains of glucose.

variants.stem: The enzyme lipase most likely digests which type of macromolecule?
A researcher isolates an enzyme called lipase. Which substrate would she expect it to break down?
Enzyme names often hint at their targets. Lipase would be expected to act on:
Which macromolecule is broken down in the small intestine by pancreatic lipase?
Lipase would be most useful in digesting which food component?
Which of these is the correct substrate for the enzyme lipase?
Fatty acids and glycerol are released when lipase acts on which macromolecule?
An enzyme whose name begins with "lip-" and ends with "-ase" most likely digests which type of molecule?

questions.why: The ending "-ase" marks an enzyme, and the beginning of the name hints at its substrate. Lipase breaks down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.
questions.deep: Use name clues: lactase → lactose, sucrase → sucrose, amylase → amylose (starch), protease → protein, nuclease → nucleic acids. Lipids are broken down by lipase; carbohydrates by enzymes such as amylase; proteins by proteases.

variants.stem: During protein digestion, amino acids are broken down to yield urea, carbon dioxide, and energy in the form of ATP. This process is an example of:
Which term describes metabolic reactions that break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy?
The breakdown of glycogen into glucose is an example of:
Which type of metabolism is the opposite of anabolism?
Digesting a starch molecule into individual glucose units is an example of which type of metabolism?
Which term describes the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones?
Cellular respiration breaks glucose into carbon dioxide and water and releases energy. This is an example of:
When the body breaks down fat to obtain energy, which type of metabolism is taking place?

questions.why: Catabolism breaks large molecules into smaller ones and releases energy. Breaking amino acids into urea, carbon dioxide, and ATP energy is an example.
questions.deep: Metabolism = anabolism + catabolism. Anabolism builds big molecules from small ones and requires energy (for example, making proteins or photosynthesis). Catabolism breaks things down and releases energy. Memory aid: Catabolism = Cutting down.

variants.stem: Which condition is most likely to denature an enzyme?
opts: A temperature far above its optimum
Adding more of the same enzyme

variants.stem: Enzymes are proteins that can lose their 3D shape. Which change would most likely cause this?
opts: Heating well above the optimum temperature

variants.stem: An enzyme works best at pH 6 and 37 °C. Which condition would most likely denature it?
A protein loses its three-dimensional structure and stops functioning when exposed to which of the following?
Which is most likely to cause an enzyme's active site to change shape and lose function?
Cooking an egg turns the clear protein white because the protein is exposed to which condition?
Which of the following would cause the greatest loss of enzyme activity due to denaturation for a human enzyme?
opts: Keeping it at its optimum pH

variants.stem: An enzyme's activity falls to nearly zero because its shape has unraveled. Which cause is most likely?
opts: Exposure to extreme heat or pH

questions.why: Extreme temperature or pH breaks the bonds that hold an enzyme in its 3D shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate and the enzyme stops working (denaturation).
questions.deep: Each enzyme has an optimum pH and temperature (for many human enzymes around 37 °C). Too high a temperature or too extreme a pH denatures it. Cold slows an enzyme but usually does not unravel its shape. Denatured = unfolded and not functional.

variants.stem: Which molecule forms the double layer that makes up the cell membrane?
Which type of molecule has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails?
Which molecule is the main structural component of cell membranes?
The cell membrane is a bilayer made mostly of which molecule?
Which molecule has a glycerol backbone, a phosphate group, and two fatty acid chains?
In a cell membrane, hydrophobic tails face inward away from water. Which molecule has these tails?
Which lipid is amphipathic, with one end that attracts water and one end that repels it?
Which molecule is found in large quantities in the plasma membrane of a cell?

questions.why: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails. They arrange in two layers (a bilayer) to form the cell membrane.
questions.deep: In water, the heads face outward toward the watery environment and the tails tuck inward, away from water. Proteins and cholesterol are embedded in the bilayer. This structure makes the membrane selectively permeable.

variants.stem: A nucleotide from DNA is composed of which three components?
opts: Deoxyribose sugar, phosphate group, nitrogenous base
Ribose sugar, phosphate group, nitrogenous base
Deoxyribose sugar, amino acid, fatty acid
Ribose sugar, amino acid, fatty acid

variants.stem: Which set correctly lists the parts of one DNA nucleotide?
The monomer of DNA contains a nitrogenous base, a phosphate group, and which sugar?
Which sugar is part of each nucleotide in DNA?
DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. Which sugar does the name refer to?
In a strand of DNA, each repeating unit includes a phosphate, a nitrogenous base, and what else?
Which description matches the monomer that makes up DNA?
Which molecule is the building block of DNA?
opts: A nucleotide with deoxyribose, a phosphate, and a base
A nucleotide with ribose, a phosphate, and a base
An amino acid with an amine and a carboxyl group
A fatty acid attached to a glycerol backbone

questions.why: A DNA nucleotide consists of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (A, T, G, or C).
questions.deep: DNA = DeoxyriboNucleic Acid, so its sugar is deoxyribose. RNA = RiboNucleic Acid, so its sugar is ribose. The nitrogenous base is the "letter" part of the nucleotide. Nucleotides link through their sugar and phosphate groups to form the strand.

variants.stem: Shortly after fertilization, the first cells (blastomeres) can become any type of cell, including placental tissue. Which term describes them?
Which term describes a cell that can develop into a complete organism?
A zygote and the early cells from its first few divisions are best described as:
Which cells have the greatest developmental potential, able to form all tissues, including those outside the embryo itself?
Cells that can become any cell of the body and also the placenta are called:
The earliest cells of an embryo after fertilization can give rise to a whole organism. Which term describes this ability?
Which type of potency is shown by a fertilized egg?
Which level of potency is the highest, above pluripotent and multipotent?

questions.why: Totipotent cells, such as the zygote and the first blastomeres, can differentiate into any cell type and can form a whole organism.
questions.deep: Potency from greatest to least: totipotent (everything, including placenta) → pluripotent (all body cell types, such as embryonic stem cells) → multipotent (a limited family of cells, such as blood stem cells) → unipotent (one cell type). Memory aid: Toti = Total.

variants.stem: What is chromatin?
opts: An enzyme complex that copies DNA
A structure that carries RNA to the ribosome
A network of protein fibers that shapes the cell

variants.stem: Which description matches chromatin in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell?
opts: A complex that makes copies of DNA
A carrier of RNA out of the nucleus
Fibers that hold the cell's shape

variants.stem: Which statement about histones and DNA is correct?
opts: DNA wraps around histones to form chromatin
Histones carry RNA out of the nucleus
Histones are fibers that give the cell shape

variants.stem: How is DNA organized so that it fits inside the nucleus?
opts: It wraps around histone proteins as chromatin
It forms a ring made of RNA
It is spread loosely across the cytoplasm

variants.stem: Which best defines chromatin?
opts: A complex of DNA and histone proteins
A complex of RNA and ribosomes

variants.stem: Chromatin condenses into chromosomes before cell division. What is chromatin made of?
Which structure is formed when DNA is wound around histone proteins?
What does chromatin consist of?

questions.why: Chromatin is DNA wrapped around histone proteins, which keeps the long DNA molecule organized and tightly packed in the nucleus.
questions.deep: Chromatin (loosely packed) condenses into visible chromosomes during cell division. Think of histones as spools and DNA as thread. DNA replication is done by enzymes such as helicase and DNA polymerase, not by chromatin.

variants.stem: A double-stranded DNA molecule contains 15% adenine. What percent of the molecule is guanine? Give a whole number.
In a sample of double-stranded DNA, adenine makes up 15% of the bases. According to Chargaff's rules, what percent of the bases are guanine?
A segment of double-stranded DNA is 15% thymine. What percent is cytosine? Give a whole number.
If 15% of the nucleotides in a double-stranded DNA sample are adenine, what percent are guanine? Give a whole number.
Double-stranded DNA from a bacterium is 15% adenine. Use Chargaff's rules to find the percent of cytosine.
In double-stranded DNA, adenine and thymine together make up 30% of the bases. What percent are guanine? Give a whole number.
A researcher finds that 15% of the bases in a DNA double helix are adenine. What percent of the bases are guanine? Give a whole number.
Thymine accounts for 15% of the bases in a double-stranded DNA sample. What percent of the bases are guanine?

questions.why: By Chargaff's rules, A = T and G = C. If A = 15%, then T = 15%, leaving 70% for G + C, so G = 35% (and C = 35%).
questions.deep: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine, so their amounts are equal. All four bases add up to 100%. Chargaff's rules apply to double-stranded DNA, not to single-stranded RNA.

variants.stem: RNA is unique from DNA in all of the following ways EXCEPT:
opts: Its nucleotides contain a phosphate group
Its nucleotides contain the sugar ribose

variants.stem: All of the following are differences between RNA and DNA EXCEPT:
opts: Both have nucleotides containing phosphate groups
RNA has uracil while DNA has thymine
RNA is usually single-stranded while DNA is double-stranded
RNA has ribose while DNA has deoxyribose

variants.stem: Which feature do RNA and DNA share?
opts: Nucleotides that contain a phosphate group

variants.stem: Which of the following is NOT a difference between RNA and DNA?
RNA and DNA are alike in which way?
opts: Each nucleotide has a phosphate group

variants.stem: Which statement is true of both RNA and DNA?
opts: Their nucleotides contain a phosphate group

variants.stem: Which property does NOT distinguish RNA from DNA?
Choose the statement that is true for both RNA and DNA.
opts: Both are made of nucleotides with a phosphate group

questions.why: Both RNA and DNA are made of nucleotides that contain a phosphate group. The differences are the sugar (ribose vs. deoxyribose), one base (uracil vs. thymine), and the number of strands (usually single vs. double).
questions.deep: On the TEAS, watch for EXCEPT and NOT questions: you are looking for the false statement (or the shared feature). RNA = ribose, uracil, usually single-stranded. DNA = deoxyribose, thymine, double-stranded helix.

variants.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a solution with a very high salt concentration. What will happen?
opts: Water will leave the cell and the cell will shrink
Water will enter the cell and the cell will swell
Salt will enter the cell and the cell will swell
The cell will keep its size

variants.stem: A red blood cell is placed in a hypertonic solution. Which will occur?
opts: Water leaves the cell and the cell shrinks
Water enters the cell and the cell swells
Solute enters the cell and the cell swells
The cell stays the same size

variants.stem: Water moves by osmosis when a red blood cell is placed in concentrated salt water. The cell will:
The solution surrounding a red blood cell has much more solute than the cell's cytoplasm. What happens to the cell?
Which describes the net movement of water when a red blood cell is placed in very salty water?
A red blood cell is placed in water that is much saltier than its cytoplasm. Which is the result?
What happens to a red blood cell in a hypertonic environment?
Because salt cannot cross the membrane, what happens to a red blood cell in a very salty solution?
opts: Water leaves and the cell shrinks
Water enters and the cell expands
Salt enters and the cell expands
The cell neither gains nor loses water

questions.why: Salt cannot easily cross the membrane, so water moves by osmosis toward the saltier side. In a very salty solution water leaves the red blood cell and the cell shrinks.
questions.deep: Water moves from lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration. Pure water (hypotonic): water enters the red blood cell and it swells and may burst. Very salty solution (hypertonic): water leaves and the cell shrinks. Isotonic: no net change.

variants.stem: A heterozygous parent (Aa) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (aa). What percent of the offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive? Give a whole number.
In a certain animal, albino (a) is recessive to normal coat color (A). A heterozygous animal mates with an albino animal. What percent of the offspring are expected to be albino? Give a whole number.
A Punnett square crosses Bb × bb. What percent of the offspring have the genotype bb? Give a whole number.
A parent with genotype Tt is crossed with a parent with genotype tt. What is the probability, as a percent, that a child has genotype tt? Give a whole number.
One parent is a carrier (Cc) for a recessive trait and the other parent has the recessive trait (cc). What percent of their offspring are expected to show the trait? Give a whole number.
A cross is made between Rr and rr plants. What percent of the offspring are expected to be rr? Give a whole number.
If an Aa individual mates with an aa individual, what percent of the offspring will be aa? Give a whole number.
A carrier (Dd) and an affected individual (dd) have children. What is the percent chance that each child is dd? Give a whole number.

questions.why: Aa × aa gives 2 Aa : 2 aa, so half (50%) of the offspring are homozygous recessive (aa).
questions.deep: Set up the Punnett square: one parent's alleles across the top, the other's down the side. Aa × aa → Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Genotype ratio 1:1, so 50% Aa (heterozygous) and 50% aa. Compare with Aa × Aa, which gives 25% aa.

variants.stem: After Gram staining, bacteria with a thick peptidoglycan cell wall will appear what color?
Gram-positive bacteria stain which color?
A bacterium has a thick outer peptidoglycan layer. Under a light microscope after Gram staining, it will look:
Which color do Gram-positive cells appear after the Gram stain procedure?
Gram staining sorts bacteria by cell wall structure. Which color results for cells with a thick peptidoglycan layer on the outside?
Staphylococcus epidermidis is Gram-positive. How will it appear after Gram staining?
On a Gram-stained slide, which color is characteristic of Gram-positive bacteria?
A Gram-positive bacterium retains the crystal violet dye. What color will it be?

questions.why: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick outer layer of peptidoglycan that holds the crystal violet dye, so they stain purple.
questions.deep: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer sandwiched between membranes and stain pink/red. Memory aid: Gram-Positive = Purple. Gram staining helps identify bacteria, which guides which antibiotics to use.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which of the following diseases are caused by viruses?
Select all that apply: Which are viral infections?
Select all that apply: Which diseases are caused by viruses rather than bacteria?
Select all that apply: Which of the following are NOT caused by viruses?
Select all that apply: Antibiotics would be ineffective against which of these?
opts: Urinary tract infection caused by E. coli

variants.stem: Select all that apply: Which diseases are caused by viruses?
Select all that apply: Which of these illnesses are viral?
Select all that apply: Which of the following infections are caused by viruses?

questions.why: Measles, herpes, influenza, chickenpox, mumps, polio, rabies, hepatitis, and HIV are viral. Pertussis, tuberculosis, strep throat, and cholera are bacterial; malaria is caused by a protozoan; candidiasis and ringworm are fungal.
questions.deep: Match the pathogen to the drug: antibiotics (bactericidal) treat bacteria, antivirals treat viruses, antifungals (such as fluconazole) treat fungi, and antiprotozoal drugs (such as metronidazole) treat protozoa. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. Viruses are smaller than bacteria.

variants.stem: A reaction releases heat to its surroundings, and the container feels warm. What type of reaction is this?
The combustion of methane gives off heat and light. This reaction is classified as:
Which term describes a reaction in which the products have less energy than the reactants and energy is released?
A chemical reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, and the temperature of the surroundings rises. Which type is it?
Which type of reaction releases energy, usually as heat?
An instant hot pack heats up when it is activated. The reaction inside is:
Which of the following describes an exothermic reaction?
opts: It releases heat to the surroundings
It absorbs heat from the surroundings
It occurs only in living cells

variants.stem: In an energy diagram, the products are lower in energy than the reactants. Which type of reaction is this?

questions.why: An exothermic reaction releases energy (usually as heat) to the surroundings because the products have less energy than the reactants.
questions.deep: Exothermic: heat released, surroundings warm up (combustion, hot packs, cellular respiration). Endothermic: heat absorbed, surroundings cool down (instant cold packs, photosynthesis). Memory aid: Exo = exit (heat exits); Endo = enters.

variants.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same number of ____ but different numbers of ____.
How do carbon-12 and carbon-14 differ?
opts: They have different numbers of neutrons
They have different numbers of protons

variants.stem: Which statement correctly describes isotopes of the same element?
opts: Same atomic number, different mass number
Same mass number, different atomic number

variants.stem: Two atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. They are:
Hydrogen, deuterium, and tritium all have one proton. They differ in the number of:
What distinguishes one isotope of an element from another?
Atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons are called:
Which pair of atoms are isotopes of each other?
opts: 6 protons and 6 neutrons; 6 protons and 8 neutrons
6 protons and 6 neutrons; 7 protons and 6 neutrons
6 protons and 6 neutrons; 8 protons and 8 neutrons
7 protons and 7 neutrons; 8 protons and 8 neutrons

questions.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons, same atomic number) that have different numbers of neutrons, and therefore different mass numbers.
questions.deep: The number of protons defines the element. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, carbon-14 has 8, and both have 6 protons. Isotopes have nearly identical chemical behavior but different masses; some are radioactive. Ions differ in electrons, not neutrons.

variants.stem: Tap the point on the curve where enzyme activity is highest.
Tap the part of the graph that shows the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Tap the peak of the curve.
Tap the location where the enzyme is working at its best.
Tap the temperature at which this enzyme shows its greatest activity.
Tap the point where the enzyme is most active, just before activity begins to fall because of denaturation.
Tap the highest point on the activity curve.
Tap the spot on the graph that marks the optimal condition for the enzyme.

questions.why: The enzyme is most active at the peak of the curve, which marks its optimum temperature. Activity falls on either side of it.
questions.deep: Read a graph by first identifying the axes: here, temperature on the x-axis and enzyme activity on the y-axis. At temperatures well above the optimum the enzyme starts to denature, so activity drops. Below the optimum, the enzyme works slowly but is not usually denatured.

variants.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data in the table?
opts: The enzyme is most active near 37 °C and much less active at higher temperatures
Enzyme activity increases at every temperature tested
The enzyme shows no activity below 30 °C

variants.stem: Based on the table, which statement is accurate?
opts: Activity peaks near 37 °C, then drops at higher temperatures
Activity rises as the temperature rises from 20 °C to 55 °C
The highest activity is recorded at 55 °C

variants.stem: A student records enzyme activity at five temperatures. Which statement does the data support?
opts: The enzyme performs best at about 37 °C
The enzyme performs best at about 20 °C
The enzyme performs best at about 55 °C
The enzyme is unaffected by temperature

variants.stem: Which is the best interpretation of the results shown?
opts: The optimum temperature is near 37 °C, and activity declines past it
The enzyme is fully inactive at 30 °C
Activity is the same at every temperature

variants.stem: What do the data suggest about the effect of temperature on this enzyme?
opts: Activity is highest near 37 °C and falls at higher temperatures
Temperature has no effect on activity

variants.stem: Which statement correctly describes the trend in enzyme activity?
opts: Activity rises to a peak near 37 °C, then falls
Activity rises at every temperature tested
Activity falls at every temperature tested
Activity stays constant across all temperatures

variants.stem: Which statement matches the information in the table?
opts: Activity at 37 °C is greater than activity at 45 °C
Activity at 55 °C is greater than activity at 37 °C
Activity at 20 °C is greater than activity at 30 °C
Activity at 45 °C is greater than activity at 37 °C

variants.stem: Which claim can be made using only the data in the table?
opts: The enzyme is most active at 37 °C among the temperatures tested
The enzyme is most active at 55 °C among the temperatures tested
The enzyme is most active at 20 °C among the temperatures tested
The enzyme is equally active at all temperatures tested

questions.why: Activity is highest at 37 °C (45 units) and drops at 45 °C and 55 °C, so the data support an optimum near 37 °C with decreasing activity at higher temperatures.
questions.deep: When a question says the answer must be supported by the table, only use the numbers given. Note what the data does NOT show: it has no measurements between listed temperatures, so claims such as "exactly 37 °C is the best possible temperature" go beyond the data.

variants.stem: A student adds iodine solution to a potato slice, and the slice turns dark blue-black. Which statement is an observation?
opts: The potato slice turned dark blue-black
The potato is a good energy source

variants.stem: A student adds iodine solution to a potato slice, and the slice turns dark blue-black. Which statement describes what was directly seen rather than a conclusion drawn from it?
opts: The slice changed to dark blue-black

variants.stem: A student adds iodine to a potato slice, and the slice turns dark blue-black. Which of the following is NOT an inference?
opts: The potato slice turned dark blue-black
The iodine reacted with something in the potato
The color change means a chemical was present

variants.stem: A student reports four statements about a potato slice treated with iodine. Which one is based directly on what was seen?
opts: The iodine solution is an indicator
The color shows starch is present

variants.stem: A student adds iodine to a potato slice and the slice turns dark blue-black. Which statement belongs in the observations section of a lab notebook?
opts: The potato slice became dark blue-black
The test proves the potato is nutritious

variants.stem: After iodine is added to a potato slice, the slice turns dark blue-black. Which is a direct observation, not an explanation?
opts: The potato slice turned a dark blue-black color
The potato slice contains starch molecules
The potato slice is a plant storage organ

variants.stem: Iodine is added to a potato slice and the slice turns dark blue-black. Which statement reports data without interpreting it?
opts: The color change shows a starch test
Starch is present in the slice
The slice is rich in carbohydrates

variants.stem: A potato slice turns dark blue-black after iodine is added. Which of the following is an observation instead of an inference?
opts: The surface of the potato slice turned dark blue-black
The potato slice has complex carbohydrates
The potato is a starchy food

questions.why: An observation records what is directly seen, measured, or heard (the slice turned dark blue-black). An inference is a conclusion based on the observation and prior knowledge (the potato contains starch).
questions.deep: Observations: facts gathered with the senses or instruments (qualitative or quantitative). Inferences: explanations or conclusions that go beyond the data. Hypotheses are testable predictions, and models are simplified descriptions of systems. On the TEAS, ask yourself: could I see or measure this directly?
